title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used one hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed all planned pairs (complete_pair_count = 200) and consumed 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. The paired contingency was n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because baseline validator‑detectable failures were absent on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, exact execution accounting (model_calls_used = 200; repair_calls_used = 0), the Mininet 10% holdout (20 tasks) that produced zero validator–emulator disagreements, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of methodological tradeoffs, threats to validity, and operational implications (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises productivity gains for network operators but creates risk when a generated configuration violates workflow constraints, service‑continuity requirements, or vendor/device semantics. Recent work therefore proposes grounding and verification layers—generate–validate–repair (GVR) or similar verifier‑assisted loops—to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. However, the operational benefit of automated repair depends on (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures given a fixed generation policy, (ii) validator coverage and fidelity, and (iii) the repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered and executed a tightly scoped confirmatory question: Does an automated deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? Our contribution is an externally auditable, preregistered paired experiment that fixes the generator output per task to isolate the marginal effect of invoking validation and (if required) a single automated repair.
sections.related_work: Prior surveys and empirical studies document that LLMs make factual errors and are sensitive to prompt design and sampling; mitigation strategies include retrieval grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, constrained agent designs, and guarded tool registries. In NetOps, prototype systems demonstrate feasibility of intent→configuration translation but rarely provide instrumented, preregistered failure‑rate studies that isolate the marginal effect of deterministic validators plus repairs. Red‑team and audit literature also documents configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection vectors that can alter safety outcomes; these motivate conservative validator/emulator corroboration in operational pipelines. Our experiment sits at the intersection: it is not a broad benchmark across many models or sampling regimes but a confirmatory paired test of whether deterministic repair reduces validator‑observable failures for a fixed model and generation policy.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and high‑level design. The study was preregistered (id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) as a paired binary experiment with n = 200 tasks. For each task a single deterministic initial candidate was produced and reused for both conditions (shared_initial design). Conditions: (A) baseline — LLM‑only application of the shared candidate to the primary deterministic validator; (B) guarded (GVR) — the same shared candidate validated and, if the validator reported violations, allowed at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM, followed by re‑validation. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, tested with an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs used 10,000 resamples with bootstrap_seed = 1729 (as recorded and executed). Power planning assumed a baseline unsafe incidence ≈30% and a targeted 50% relative reduction to justify n = 200; these were planning assumptions only.

Task bank, validators, and holdout. The task bank comprised 200 machine‑checkable intent→configuration problems across four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 each). Each task encoded initial and expected final states plus workflow constraints (make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields, group minima) and a required_sequence. The primary deterministic checker enforced syntactic and intent/constraint checks (validator reported a boolean valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, and difficulty labels such as "medium", "hard", "very_hard"). As a preregistered secondary corroboration, a Mininet data‑plane emulator was run on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches.

Adapter and sampling semantics; determinism reconciliation. The hosted adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics that produced one model invocation per task and reused that output for both baseline and guarded conditions; this design removed sampling variance across conditions so the paired contrast isolates the marginal effect of validation/repair on an identical generator output. The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses). The recorded model configuration lists "temperature": null; despite this field value, determinism for the confirmatory estimand was achieved by adapter enforcement of single shared initial generations and by the adapter’s call accounting policy (one initial generation per task, at most one repair call when invoked). Deterministic accounting artifacts report hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming single shared invocations per task and total model_calls_used = 200. These concrete numeric execution facts (model_calls_used = 200; repair_calls_used = 0) are reported here because they bear directly on causal interpretation: no multiple draws, re‑sampling, or stochastic candidate diversification were permitted by the preregistered design.

Statistical tests, exclusions, and contamination plan. The primary test was an exact McNemar two‑sided test on the 2×2 paired table (n11, n10, n01, n00). Pairs where both conditions failed due to infrastructure errors would have been excluded deterministically; the preregistered contamination plan excluded pairs where the primary validator disagreed with the Mininet emulator. The randomized Mininet holdout executed as planned and reported zero validator–emulator disagreement flags in that 20‑task sample. A documented reproducibility gap exists: the artifact set does not include a labeled selection seed for the Mininet holdout draw, which prevents bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of which exact tasks comprised the holdout despite the contamination summary reporting zero disagreements; we disclose this gap explicitly and discuss its interpretive effect below.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and raw outcomes. The autonomous run completed all planned episodes and pairs. Accounting: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions), complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200, maximum_model_calls = 400 (preregistered cap), repair_calls_used = 0. The adapter/provider accounting shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, consistent with the enforced shared_initial semantics. No technical failures or unscorable episodes occurred.

Primary paired outcome. Every shared initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) yields a 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because there were no discordant pairs, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis cannot be evaluated on this sample: there were no baseline validator‑detectable failures for GVR to reduce.

Secondary corroboration and diagnostics. The randomized 10% Mininet holdout (20 tasks) produced zero disagreements between the primary validator verdicts and emulator checks (zero contamination flags observed). Representative per‑task validator traces show parsed_command_count equalled required_command_count in validated outputs and difficulty labels such as "make_before_break_uplink_switchover", "paired_link_atomic_mtu_change", and "rolling_access_vlan_migration", indicating the task bank exercised nontrivial dependency patterns even when outputs were validator‑satisfying. Because no validator failures occurred, preregistered secondary estimands (average repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) are empty for this run.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The confirmatory null result is artifact‑grounded and interpretable: under the preregistered fixed generation policy (single shared deterministic generation per task) and with the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini) and prompts, the primary deterministic validator detected zero initial failures across the 200 tasks. This outcome implies the marginal value of automated validator‑guided repair was zero for validator‑detectable errors on this workload and generation policy. It does not imply repair is globally useless; rather, GVR utility is workload‑ and sampling‑policy dependent.

Design tradeoffs and external validity. The paired shared_initial design intentionally isolates the causal effect of validation/repair on an identical generator output, at the cost of excluding benefits that could arise from re‑sampling the LLM (multiple draws per condition) or from stochastic sampling (nonzero temperature). For practical operational assessments of unconditional failure risk, independent per‑condition multi‑sample designs better estimate the probability an LLM pipeline produces an unsafe candidate on any application. External validity is further constrained by testing a single hosted model, a single validator implementation, and a curated task bank; different models, prompt regimes, larger repair budgets, or adversarial inputs could produce different outcomes.

Validator coverage and reproducibility caveat. Deterministic validators are necessary but not sufficient oracles for operational safety; they encode a definable set of checks and can miss device idiosyncrasies or emergent failure modes only visible in larger emulation or real‑device tests. The Mininet 10% holdout corroboration found no validator–emulator disagreements in the sampled 20 tasks, which increases confidence in validator coverage for that small sample. However, the documented reproducibility gap—the absence of a labeled seed for the Mininet holdout selection—means exact reconstruction of the holdout draw is not possible from the labeled artifacts, limiting the strength of cross‑audit claims based on that holdout despite the zero‑disagreement observation; we disclose this limitation and recommend future runs record holdout selection seeds to enable precise reconstruction.

Practical recommendations. Teams considering GVR should first measure baseline validator failure prevalence for their intended generation policy and workload: when baseline validator‑detectable failures are rare under the chosen generator/prompt pair, the marginal safety return from a narrow single‑repair GVR loop is small and resources may be better spent improving validator fidelity, expanding emulation checks, or enabling multi‑sample generation to surface latent failures. When baseline failures are nontrivial, GVR with larger repair budgets, multi‑step repairs, or human‑in‑the‑loop escalation can reduce validator‑detectable errors; future confirmatory work should preregister designs that permit multi‑sample draws and larger repair budgets to evaluate those settings.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200), producing an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because baseline validator failures were absent, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. The artifact‑grounded outcome clarifies that GVR’s marginal benefit is conditional on baseline failure prevalence and validator coverage: for workloads and generator/prompt policies with rare validator‑detectable failures, a narrow single‑repair GVR yields no measured reduction in validator‑detected errors. Future evaluations should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, expand validator fidelity and emulation checks (with recorded selection seeds), evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model policies, and explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets to characterize operational gains.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Execution accounting: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan (start: 2026‑08‑30T11:50:34.530059Z; end: 2026‑08‑30T12:12:07.541650Z); model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task) and repair_calls_used = 0. Adapter/provider accounting recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming single shared invocations per task. A Mininet‑based emulator was preregistered and executed as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks); that holdout produced zero validator–emulator disagreements in the sampled run. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the randomized selection seed identifying which tasks comprised the Mininet 10% holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archive; this absence prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of the drawn holdout despite the contamination summary reporting no disagreements. The master prompt archive reference above is the immutable prompt required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (model_calls_used = 200; stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
